analysis.one_liner: Requires credit card grace periods to start on the statement mailing date, limiting surprise interest charges.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 11 House cosponsors, got one subcommittee hearing but never a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Truth in Lending Act so that, on any credit card that offers an interest-free grace period, that grace period must be counted from the date the monthly statement is postmarked. Card companies sometimes started the clock on an earlier date, so a customer who paid the full balance could still be charged interest on money borrowed before the statement was even mailed. The bill would have blocked issuers from using any date earlier than the postmark as the start of the grace period.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who carry credit cards with grace periods — especially people who pay their balance in full each month but were still being charged finance charges because the issuer counted the grace period from a date before the statement was mailed. They would get more interest-free days to pay, measured from when the bill was actually sent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders who pay in full

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Truth in Lending Act to prohibit a credit card issuer from treating any date before the statement's postmark as the billing date for a grace period, so the interest-free window starts when the bill is actually mailed.

For cardholders who pay their full balance, this closes a gap where issuers could start the grace period early and accrue finance charges on purchases from a statement the customer had not yet received or had little time to pay.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and card companies that offered grace-period cards — would lose some interest revenue, since customers would get more days to pay without finance charges. Issuers could try to make that up through higher rates or fees for all cardholders.

drawbacks.text: The fix is narrow: it applies only to cards that already offer a grace period. It does not require issuers to offer one, cap interest rates, or limit fees, so cards with no grace period at all are untouched.
The added interest-free days cost issuers revenue, and card companies could offset that by raising rates or fees for cardholders generally, leaving some consumers no better off.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A well-targeted but modest consumer fix. For cardholders who pay in full, it eliminates a genuinely unfair practice — being charged interest on a bill that had not reached them yet — at a real but limited cost to issuers. It does nothing about high interest rates, fees, or cards with no grace period, so it is a fairness patch rather than broader credit card reform.

outcome.mechanism: After one subcommittee hearing, the House Banking Committee never brought the bill up, and it quietly died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Lawrence Smith of Florida introduced the bill on February 27, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs.
Eleven members cosponsored it — 10 Democrats and 1 Republican.
On March 15, 1991, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage, which held a hearing on October 9, 1991.
No further action was taken — no markup, no committee vote, no House floor vote — and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: the bill never became law, so they kept setting grace period start dates on their own terms and collecting finance charges on balances customers believed they had paid off.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Card Grace Period Act of 1991 to start grace periods on the statement postmark date.

for.name: 11 House cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the only recorded signal is the cosponsor list: 10 Democrats and 1 Republican.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and card companies)
industries.note: The bill would cost issuers interest revenue by forcing grace periods to run from the statement postmark date, ending the practice of charging finance charges on balances customers had little or no time to pay interest-free. Issuers profit from the current early billing dates, so their interest in this bill ran against cardholders'.
